translation_en:
Record of Metropolitan Graduates of the Eighth Year of the Xuande Reign (1433)

Imperial Pronouncements

In the [eighth year of the] Xuande reign … Minister of Rites [your servant] Hu Ying 胡濙 … at the Fengtian Gate … regarding … the ninety-nine candidates who passed the [Metropolitan] Examination; having examined … [Minister of] Personnel … Grand Secretary of the Huagai Hall … [?], and concurrently Grand Secretary of the Jinshen [Hall] … officials. Regarding the qualifications and ranks for metropolitan graduates (jinshi): in the First Class, [in accordance with the precedent established by] Emperor Taizu Gaohuangdi … the second and third places, three candidates are selected: the first place is ranked 6b, the second [and third places of the First Class are ranked 7a? — text garbled: "Second Class ranked 7b, bestowed 7th rank"], bestowed the title of Metropolitan Graduate with Honors (jinshi jidi); the Second Class [is ranked 7b, bestowed the title of Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi chushen) — text garbled: "bestowed Associate Metropolitan Graduate, Metropolitan Graduate"]; the Third Class is ranked 8a, [bestowed the title of Associate Metropolitan Graduate (tong jinshi chushen)] … Received the Imperial Edict: "Approved." Respect this!

Readers of the Examination Papers … …

translation_en:
Sequence of Imperial Favors and Honors

Early on the first day of the third month of the eighth year of the Xuande reign (1433), the tribute scholars (gongshi) proceeded to the Inner Palace for the Palace Examination. The Emperor took his seat in the Fengtian Hall and personally bestowed the policy question.

Early on the third day, the civil and military officials attended in court dress in their ceremonial ranks. On this day, the Embroidered-uniform Guard at the Auxiliary Administration set up the imperial insignia arrays upon the vermilion steps and within the vermilion courtyard. The Emperor took his seat in the Fengtian Hall, and officials of the Court of State Ceremonial at the Auxiliary Administration transmitted the imperial decree and called out the names of the successful candidates. Officials of the Ministry of Rites at the Auxiliary Administration bore the yellow placard in both hands, led along the way by drums and music, and went out beyond the Left Chang'an Gate to post it on display. Once this was completed, officials of Shuntian Prefectural Administration used a ceremonial parasol and retinue to escort the Principal Graduate (zhuangyuan) back to his residence.

Your servant has heard that the governance of the sages is rooted in the Way, and the Way of the sages is made manifest in the Classics. For governance is rooted in the Way, and the origin of the Way issues from Heaven; the Way is made manifest in the Classics, and the essentials of the Classics converge in the mind. Thus Heaven is that from which the Way issues, and the mind is that wherein principle is fully endowed. The sages embodied this principle and composed the Classics to hand down teachings to the world; the worthies illuminated this principle and wrote books to instruct people—none of this was anything other than what issued from Heaven's bestowal and what was endowed in the mind.
Reverently reflecting upon Your Majesty the Emperor: endowed with the qualities of perspicacity, intelligence, and far-reaching wisdom, and complete in the virtues of sageliness, spirit-like discernment, civil attainment, and martial vigor, You have received the flourishing calendar of Great Peace and opened the auspicious destiny of cultured illumination. Your Way has ascended to the August Ultimate—it has indeed reached perfection, yet You still regard it as not yet having reached perfection; Your governance has attained harmonious brilliance—it is indeed flourishing, yet You still regard it as not yet flourishing. In moments of leisure from Your myriad affairs of state, You have furthermore summoned Your servants to the Court, graciously condescending to pose Your pure inquiry; moreover, You have raised the matter of the sages and worthies of antiquity composing the Classics and establishing teachings, and have spoken of "immersing the mind in the sages of the past and investigating the supreme Way." 才洞明□□□□奧而先天後天之旨推焉無非
以發明羲文之易也盖先天者伏羲之所畫乃
自然之數後天者文王之所演乃入用之位伏
羲之易惟一具口在其象數而天地萬物之理
陰陽始終之必欲知文王之易即今周易孔子
所為作傳者也苟□□聖人作易之本則當考
伏羲之圖欲知□□□文義則但求文王之經
孔子之傳二者□□□雜此其旨之異也然皆
天□人事之□□□□以相無也大抵道原
===
於一而易之□□□□大於備凡六十四卦三百
八十四爻無非□□人開物成務之道趨吉避凶
之方也治本於□□而洪範一篇綱舉目詳一二
三四皆經常之疇法天以治乎人者也六七八
九皆權變之疇即人以驗諸天者也而五皇極
一疇則主常制□□之主與天為徒為民之則者
也伏惟
皇帝陛下心伏羲大禹文王周孔之心道伏羲大禹
文王周孔之道神以知來知以藏往無非大易
之妙斂時五福錫厥庶民無非皇極之建故九

translation_en: The exterior of the Diagram forms the Eight Trigrams, yet its interior can also be used to arrange the Categories; the exterior of the Writing forms the Nine Categories, yet its interior can also be used to draw the Trigrams. Thus, when former Confucians said that "the Luo Writing can serve to make the Changes (Yi), and the River Diagram can also serve to make the Plan (Fan)," this is what they meant. Fuxi patterned after the River Diagram to form the trigrams: leaving empty the five and ten in its center is the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji); the odd numbers totaling twenty and the even numbers totaling twenty are the Two Modes (Liangyi); taking one, two, three, and four to make six, seven, eight, and nine are the Four Images (Sixiang); dividing the combinations of the four cardinal directions to form Qian, Kun, Li, and Kan, and filling the voids of the four corners to form Dui, Zhen, Xun, and Gen are the Eight Trigrams (Bagua). In the Luo Writing, leaving empty the five in its center is likewise the Supreme Ultimate; the odd and even numbers each occupying twenty are likewise the Two Modes; taking one, two, three, and four to contain nine, eight, seven, and six, totaling fifteen vertically and horizontally and mutually forming seven, eight, nine, and six, are likewise the Four Images; taking the regular positions of the four cardinal directions to form Qian, Kun, Kan, and Li, and the oblique positions of the four corners to form Dui, Zhen, Xun, and Gen, are likewise the Eight Trigrams. Whether the Eight Trigrams or the Nine Categories, although their methods differ, their principle is simply one and the same. Nevertheless, although the principle of the Changes had already been opened up since Fuxi drew the trigrams, it had to wait until King Wen, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius before it became clear. This is because in high antiquity there were drawings without written text; when King Wen composed the Judgments (Tuanci), the Duke of Zhou composed the Line Statements (Yaoci), and Confucius wrote the Ten Wings (Shiyi) to explain their meanings, the principle that Fuxi had revealed to humankind by drawing the trigrams thereby became ever more manifest. When Yu set forth the Great Plan (Hongfan), the Nine Categories were already arranged, yet it had to wait for Jizi before it became complete. translation_en: … "is the instruction of the Lord on High." Nothing that speaks of governance is more detailed than this, and yet it is wholly rooted in Heaven. For although the Way of the Supreme Ultimate is embodied in the ruler's own person, the verifications of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness each follow their corresponding responses, and their origin is rooted in Heaven. This being so, the purport of the transmission and creation of the Diagram, the Writing, the Changes, and the Plan has surely already been decided within the imperial mind; yet as Your Majesty still earnestly raises this to question your servants, your servant has briefly set forth its general outline. However, at the close of this essay, your servant humbly ventures to offer a further word. Fuxi drew the trigrams on the basis of the Yellow River Diagram to prepare things for the use of the people, and Yu of Xia arranged the categories on the basis of the Tortoise Writing to establish the Supreme Ultimate; it was only because their minds were in sincere accord with Heaven that they obtained the response of auspicious omens and achieved the flourishing efficacy of governance, unsurpassed throughout all antiquity. Your servant humbly prays that Your Majesty, with the mind of a great sage, will plumb the depths of the Ultimate Way: using the hexagrams to prepare things for the use of the people, so as to cause all people under Heaven to open up the resources of things and accomplish their affairs, with nothing unsuitable—which is precisely what the Book of Changes calls "spiritually transforming them so as to make them suitable for the people"; and establishing the Supreme Ultimate to manifest the Way of governance, causing all the people under Heaven to "converge on the Ultimate and return to the Ultimate"—which is precisely what the Book of Documents calls "broad and level, the Kingly Way is straight and upright." Thereby Heaven will not grudge its Way, Earth will not grudge its treasures, the seas and mountains will display their numinous power, rain and sunshine will be seasonable, the creatures of the Yellow River and the Luo River will all arrive without exception, and how could the auspicious signs of civil governance in our flourishing age differ from the responses obtained when Fuxi and Yu of Xia arose? Your servant's learning is shallow; having the undeserved honor of presenting this grand reply, without measuring my own rusticity and narrowness, I dare to set forth my foolish views, defiling Your Sacred Glance above and offending Your Heavenly Majesty, overcome with the utmost trepidation and awe.

Your servant Zhong Fu 鍾復.

After Confucius died, as the sound of the wooden bell-clapper grew faint and the teachings at the Apricot Altar ceased, the sage's [learning…] was lost. Coming down to the Song dynasty, Master Zhou of Lianxi (Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤) appeared. Without relying on a teacher's [transmission…], he composed both the Diagram (Taijitu) and the Book (Tongshu), getting to the very root of the essential principles. [In the Diagram] he said: "The Non-Ultimate and yet [the Supreme Ultimate!] In movement it generates yang; in stillness it generates yin. One movement and one stillness form each other's [root. By the division of yin and] the division of yang, the Two Modes are established. Yang transforms and yin [unites, generating water, fire, wood, metal, and earth…]." Sincerity penetrates and sincerity returns, becoming origination, flourish, advantage, [and firmness… Humanity], righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness are also the Five Phases. The essential [meaning] of the Diagram [and the Book…] was thus complete. Master Shao Kangjie (Shao Yong 邵雍), a hero among men endowed by Heaven, […grasped] from Fuxi and King Wen the purport of the Prior-to-Heaven (xiantian) and Posterior-to-Heaven (houtian) arrangements: Qian in the south and Kun in the north, Li in the east and Kan in the west, Zhen in the northeast […and Dui in the southeast] dividing [?], Xun in the southwest and Gen in the northwest; heaven and earth fix their positions, mountain and marsh communicate their vital氣, [thunder and wind] press upon each other, water and fire do not combat each other, the eight trigrams intermingle with one another to form the sixty-four hexagrams; [counting] the past goes with the flow, knowing the future goes against the flow—this is what is called the learning of Prior-to-Heaven. [As for Li in the south and Kan in the north,] Zhen in the east and Dui in the west, Xun in the southeast and Gen in the northeast, Kun in the southwest [and Qian in the northwest]; emerging in Zhen, brought into alignment in Xun, seeing one another in Li, [toiling] in [Kun, rejoicing in Dui, contending in Qian, laboring in Kan,] and brought to completion in Gen—this is what is called the learning of Posterior-to-Heaven. [The Prior-to-Heaven arrangement…] establishes its substance, while the circulating operation of the Posterior-to-Heaven arrangement wondrously…
